[**Example: an apparently silent cell and an informative population**]{#sec-foundations-count-example} Suppose the expected rate is 20 spikes per second and an observation lasts 50 ms. The expected count is $20\times0.05=1$. The probability of seeing no spike is $e^{-1}=0.368$. A silent interval is therefore common even though the expected rate is positive. Now suppose 20 conditionally independent cells each have that rate. Their total count is Poisson with mean 20 and standard deviation $\sqrt{20}=4.47$. The total rate estimate has a relative standard deviation of about 22.4%, compared with 100% for one cell. [Population averaging helps because the independent count variances add while the mean signal adds directly. If a common varying input makes several cells' firing rates rise and fall together, that shared variation will not disappear in the same way.]{.key-statement} The two count distributions can be compared on the same rate per cell scale.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-POISSON-POPULATION}}
Dividing the pooled rate estimate by 20 keeps the expected rate per cell fixed, while independent averaging reduces its relative spread. See [Poisson count likelihood, SI Eq. S43, p. 9](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=9).

[**Example: two disturbances to the same stored angle**]{#sec-foundations-attractor-example}

Consider a teaching model with two activities $r_1,r_2$ in spikes per second. Let $b=40$ spikes per second and let $k=2$ spikes per second per degree. A stored angle $\theta$ corresponds to

$$
r_1=b+k\theta,\qquad r_2=b-k\theta.
$$

The fixed points lie on the line $r_1+r_2=2b$. Restrict attention to angles where both rates remain positive. Define the deviation in their mean activity and the represented angle as

$$
x=\frac{r_1+r_2}{2}-b,
\qquad
\theta=\frac{r_1-r_2}{2k}.
$$

Suppose each activity changes according to

$$
\dot r_1=-a x,\qquad \dot r_2=-a x,
$$

where $a>0$ has units inverse seconds. Adding and subtracting these equations gives

$$
\dot x=-a x,\qquad \dot\theta=0.
$$

The first equation has solution $x(t)=x(0)e^{-at}$, so disturbances in the common activity decay. The second equation retains any angle set by the initial state.

At $\theta=5$ degrees, the rates are $(50,30)$. Compare two disturbances from this same state:

- A disturbance of $(+3,+3)$ changes the rates to $(53,33)$. It creates $x=3$ but leaves the represented angle at 5 degrees. The restoring dynamics return to $(50,30)$.
- A disturbance of $(+3,-3)$ gives $(53,27)$, with $x=0$ and angle $26/(2\times2)=6.5$ degrees. This state lies on the fixed-point line, so there is no restoring response.

[In the second case, the circuit remains coherent while holding the wrong angle.]{.key-statement}

The two changes occupy different directions in the activity plane. The solid arrow in the figure is the restoring motion produced by the model. The dashed arrow shows the imposed disturbance along the fixed-point line, rather than a deterministic restoring flow.

{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-ATTRACTOR}}

This construction illustrates the geometry; it is not a fit to eye-neuron recordings. In a larger network, the direction that survives depends on its connection weights and cannot always be found by an ordinary perpendicular projection. The [network calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) derives the correct projection from the network's linearized dynamics.

[**Example: why the noise grows slower than a fixed bias**]{#sec-foundations-diffusion-example} Take an illustrative angular diffusion coefficient $D=0.02$ degrees squared per second. At 0.35 s its variance is $0.014$ degrees squared and its root mean squared displacement is 0.118 degrees, or about 7.10 arcminutes. At 1 s the root mean squared displacement is 0.20 degrees. These are teaching values, not a new estimate from either monkey. If there is also a constant bias velocity $v=0.10$ degrees per second, then $$ \theta(t)-\theta(0)=vt+\sqrt{2D}\,W(t), \qquad \operatorname{MSD}(t)=v^2t^2+2Dt. $$ The deterministic and random contributions are equal at $t=2D/v^2=4$ seconds. Their equal contributions there are each $0.16$ degrees squared. At longer times the bias dominates this unbounded model even though it was small over a short observation. A theory of random diffusion must therefore account for systematic drift separately. Sample paths show the irregular motion; exact displacement scales show how its spread differs from a fixed bias.
{{block:fig:FOUNDATIONS-DIFFUSION-BIAS}}
A single path can turn back toward zero even while the root mean squared displacement grows. A constant bias grows linearly, so it eventually exceeds the square root growth of the random displacement scale. See [Gaussian displacement density, SI Eq. S30, p. 7](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf#page=7).

**Example: a disturbance that slides while it decays.** To see the distinction without a neural simulation, consider the local system $$ \dot x=ay,\qquad \dot y=-\lambda y,\quad\lambda>0. $$ Every point with $y=0$ is fixed. Starting from $(x_0,y_0)$ gives $y(t)=y_0e^{-\lambda t}$ and $$ x(\infty)=x_0+\frac{a}{\lambda}y_0. $$ Here $\mathbf u=(1,0)^T$ and $\mathbf v=(1,a/\lambda)^T$. A vertical perturbation changes the final memory whenever $a\ne0$. A perpendicular projection would miss that change. This is a teaching example of the projection geometry, not an additional network used in the paper.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-TILTED-DECAY}}
As y decays, x changes by one; the left vector extracts that lasting shift.

**Example: the same diffusion with a looser information bound.** In the two cell mutual inhibition model, use $b=200$ activation units and $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$. The memory coordinate is an activation difference, not an angle. At $\theta=0$ both rates are $1000\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and their slopes are $\pm5\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ per activation unit. Thus $$ J=\frac{25}{1000}+\frac{25}{1000}=0.05, \qquad D=\frac{b}{2\tau}=1000. $$ Here $J$ has units of inverse activation unit squared per second, and $D$ has activation unit squared per second. The bound is $1/(2\tau^2J)=1000$, so equality holds at this balanced state. At $\theta=100$, the rates become $1500$ and $500\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, while their slopes stay $\pm5$. Now $$ J=\frac{25}{1500}+\frac{25}{500}=\frac1{15}\simeq0.06667, \qquad \frac1{2\tau^2J}=750. $$ The actual diffusion remains $1000$. The inequality is strict because these two unequal rates no longer align the network's projection weights with the information optimal weights. This also shows why equality at a special state does not force the transfer function to be exponential on its whole domain. A constant lower bound attained everywhere and an accidental equality at one state are different claims.
{{block:fig:MEMORY-BOUND-STRICTNESS}}
The gap at $\theta=100$ shows why a lower minimum allowed by the inequality is not a reduction in the network’s actual diffusion. See [Diffusion bound, Eq. 4, p. 3](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf#page=3).

**Example: limited spike access changes the useful interval.** Take $\tau=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$, $J=10{,}000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, and $D=0.005\,\mathrm{rad}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These values attain the information bound. Full access gives $L^*=0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ and limiting readout variance $0.001\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum is $0.1732\,\mathrm{s}$ with variance $0.001155\,\mathrm{rad}^2$.

If $\alpha=0.1$, then $J_{\mathrm{obs}}=1000\,\mathrm{rad}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The ideal characteristic interval becomes $0.3162\,\mathrm{s}$ and its limiting variance becomes $0.003162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. The naive optimum becomes $0.5477\,\mathrm{s}$. A two second storage delay contributes $2DT=0.020\,\mathrm{rad}^2$ in both cases, giving total ideal asymptotic variances $0.021$ and $0.023162\,\mathrm{rad}^2$. Longer observation can reduce the readout cost; it cannot undo the random displacement during the delay.

**Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with $$ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. $$ Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that $$ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. $$ One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise.
{{block:fig:EYE-SHARED-PRIVATE-VARIANCE}}
Private prediction noise enlarges the denominator of R without changing the covariance. The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10).

### Example: opposite rate changes from the same position error {#sec:SYNTHESIS-COVARIANCE-EXAMPLE} Let the local slopes of two rate curves be $f_1'=2$ Hz/m and $f_2'=-1$ Hz/m. Suppose $D=0.01$ m²/s and the interval is 0.5 s. Then the variance of the common position displacement is $2Dt=0.01$ m². The contributions to rate variance and covariance are $$ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_1)=2^2(0.01)=0.04\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, $$ $$ \operatorname{Var}(\delta R_2)=(-1)^2(0.01)=0.01\ \mathrm{Hz}^2, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\delta R_1,\delta R_2)=(2)(-1)(0.01) =-0.02\ \mathrm{Hz}^2. $$ With only this one source, the two rate changes have correlation $-1$: one rises whenever the other falls. Adding independent private noise lowers the magnitude. [The negative covariance here comes from opposite tuning slopes under a common position change. It does not establish an inhibitory connection between the cells.]{.key-statement} For the same slopes, set both expected rates to 10 Hz at the starting position. The upper plot shows the fixed rate curves; the lower plot shows their changes under a common position displacement.
{{block:fig:SYNTHESIS-SHARED-POSITION}}
Both changes are set by the same position displacement, so they occupy one direction in the two-rate plane. Independent private fluctuations would spread them away from that line.
